editorialNote: The Ahobilam Temple is associated with Narasiṃha, the man-lion avatar of Viṣṇu.
The Nava Narasiṃha Temple at Ahobilam is associated with Viṣṇu as Narasiṃha (nine forms).
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Aitareya Upaniṣad, teaching the creation of the world from the ātman, the three births of the jīva, and the prajñānaṃ brahma mahāvākya.
The Atharvaveda is associated with several śākhās (branches), including the Śāukla and Pūrṇāṣṭikā recensions.
The Badrinath Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Badarīnārāyaṇa, the presiding deity.
The Badrinath Temple celebrates Rāma-navamī as a major festival.
The Baidyanath Temple (Baba Baidyanath Dham) is one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas, dedicated to Śiva as the sovereign healer; the temple houses a natural śiva liṅga within a forest sanctuary.
The Baidyanath Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition as one of the twelve Jyotirliṅhas; its pilgrimage is especially significant during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Madhva's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Madhva.
Nimbārka's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Nimbārka.
Rāmānuja's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Rāmānuja.
Śaṅkara's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkara.
Vallabha's Bhagavad Gītā Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Vallabha.
Vibhūti Yoga: Kṛṣṇa's description of his divine manifestations and their glories.
Viśvarūpa-darśana Yoga: Arjuna's vision of Kṛṣṇa's universal form (Viśvarūpa) and cosmic form.
Bhakti Yoga: The supreme path of loving devotion to the Lord, superior to paths of knowledge and action.
Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña Vibhāga Yoga: The distinction between the field (body) and the knower of the field (soul).
Guṇa-Traya Vibhāga Yoga: The three modes of material nature and transcendence through devotion.
Puruṣottama Yoga: The teaching on the eternal soul, the supreme personality, and the path of devotion.
Daivāsura Sampad Vibhāga Yoga: The divine and demonic natures and the characteristics of godly persons.
Śraddhā-Traya Vibhāga Yoga: The three kinds of faith and the practice of yoga according to one's nature.
Mokṣa-Saṅnyāsa Yoga: The final teaching on renunciation, the results of action, and the path to liberation.
Sāṅkhya Yoga: Kṛṣṇa's teaching on the immortal soul, the nature of the self, and the paths of knowledge and action.
Karma Yoga: The teaching on selfless action and the path of unattached performance.
Jñāna-Karma Saṅgrahana Yoga: Kṛṣṇa's discourse on the transmission of knowledge and the guru-disciple lineage.
Karma-Saṅnyāsa Yoga: Further instruction on renunciation and the path of meditation.
Dhyāna Yoga: The path of meditation and the practice of mental discipline and contemplation.
Jñāna-Vijñāna Yoga: Kṛṣṇa reveals the path of knowledge and wisdom leading to the supreme reality.
Akṣara-Brahma Yoga: The teaching on the imperishable Brahman and the paths of departure at death.
Rāja-Vidya-Rāja-Guhya Yoga: Kṛṣṇa's invitation to the highest knowledge and the yoga of devotion.
The Bhagavad Gītā is divided into 18 chapters covering Kṛṣṇa's teachings on karma yoga, jñāna yoga, and bhakti yoga.
The Bhagavad Gītā teaches bhakti-yoga as a principal path, particularly in chapters 7 and 12.
The Bhagavad Gītā teaches jñāna-yoga, particularly in chapters 2 and 13.
The Bhagavad Gītā teaches karma-yoga as a principal path, particularly in chapters 2-3.
Madhva's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Madhva.
Nimbārka's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Nimbārka.
Rāmānuja's Śrī Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra is traditionally attributed to Rāmānuja.
Śaṅkara's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkara.
Vallabha's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya is traditionally attributed to Vallabha.
The Brahma Sūtra has Madhva's Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Dvaita).
The Brahma Sūtra has Nimbārka's Vedānta Pārijāta Saurabha (Bhedābheda).
The Brahma Sūtra has Vallabha's Anubhāṣya (Śuddhādvaita).
Adhyāya 2 (Avirodha): argues against rival schools and establishes the authority of the Upaniṣads.
Adhyāya 3 (Sādhana): explains the means of attaining Brahman through knowledge, devotion, and ethical conduct.
Adhyāya 4 (Phala): describes the fruit of liberation, the vision of the supreme Brahman, and the nature of the realized soul.
The Brahma Sūtra is divided into four adhyāyas (chapters) covering the nature of Brahman and the path to liberation.
Ādi Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra is the foundational Advaita Vedānta commentary establishing non-dualism.
The Brahma Sūtras discuss the concept of avidyā (nescience) in relation to Brahman.
The Brahma Sūtras systematically discuss the nature of Brahman as the ultimate reality.

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Dvaita perspective, maintaining the eternal distinction (bheda) between the independent (svatantra) Viṣṇu and the dependent (paratantra) jīvas and matter; the neti-neti negates the world's independence, not its reality as Viṣṇu's creation.

Nimbārka's commentary tradition on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Bhedābheda (Dvaitādvaita) perspective, teaching the simultaneous difference and non-difference of the jīva and Brahman, with Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa as the supreme couple.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Viśiṣṭādvaita perspective, interpreting the neti-neti as denying upādhi (limiting adjuncts) not Brahman's attributes, and emphasizing the qualified non-duality of Brahman with cit and acit.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the largest and one of the principal Upaniṣads, covering the madhu-vidyā, the yājñavalkya-maitreyī dialogue, and the neti-neti teaching.

Vallabha's Bhāṣya on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad from the Śuddhādvaita perspective, emphasizing the pure non-duality of Kṛṣṇa as Brahman, the world as His real manifestation (not māyā), and the path of puṣṭi-mārga (grace) through Kṛṣṇa-bhakti.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad discusses the law of karma and the path of action through the famous "karmaṇy akarmaā" teaching in the later sections (Chapter 5-6).
The Bṛhadīśvara Temple at Thanjavur is associated with Lord Shiva as its presiding deity.
The Bṛhadīśvara Temple celebrates Mahāśivarātri as a major festival.
The Brihadeeswar Temple at Thanjavur belongs to the Śaiva tradition, dedicated to Nataraja (Śiva as cosmic dancer).
The Chāmuṇḍā Devi Temple is one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas, where the feet of Devī fell; dedicated to the fierce form Chāmuṇḍā.
The Chāmuṇḍā Devi Temple belongs to the Śākta tradition as one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas.

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, interpreting tat tvam archaeological-survey-of-india as "you are that (servant of Viṣṇu)" — the jīva is a distinct reflection (pratibimba) of Viṣṇu, never identical; the sat-vidyā establishes Viṣṇu as the only independent reality.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, interpreting tat tvam archaeological-survey-of-india as the identity of the individual self (jīva) as a mode (prakāra) of Brahman, not absolute identity; the sat-vidyā as establishing Viṣṇu as the supreme Brahman qualified by the world.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, famous for the sat-vidyā (being), the uddālaka-śvetaketu dialogue (tat tvam archaeological-survey-of-india), and the dahara-vidyā (heart-space).
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad teaches the unity of the individual self (jīvātman) with the ultimate (paramātman) through the "tat tvam archaeological-survey-of-india" mahāvākya.
The Chidambaram Nataraja Temple is associated with Lord Shiva as Nataraja (the cosmic dancer).
The Chidambaram Nataraja Temple celebrates Mahāśivarātri with the Ananda Tandava festival.
The Divine Mother (Devī/Durgā) is celebrated during Navaratri.
The Dvārakā Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Dvārakādhīśa.
The Dvārakā Temple celebrates Janmāṣṭamī (Kṛṣṇa's birth) as its most important festival.
The Dvārakādhīśa Temple belongs to the Vaiṣṇava tradition, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Dvārkādhīśa.
Dwārka Maṭha has Śakti Pīṭha connections in some traditions, representing the Devī connection to the dual sacred sites of Dvārakā.
Dwārka Maṭha has Śākta connections through its association with the dual sacred sites of Dvārakā.
The Ekambareswarar Temple in Kanchipuram is associated with Lord Shiva as Ekambareswarar.
The Grishneshwar Temple in Maharashtra is associated with Lord Shiva as one of the twelve Jyotirlinga sites.
The Guruvayur Krishna Temple is associated with Lord Krishna (an avatar of Vishnu) as its presiding deity.
The Guruvayur Temple is associated with the Onam festival celebrations.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Īśa Upaniṣad, the shortest principal Upaniṣad (18 verses), teaching the Īśāvāsyam idam sarvam (all this is pervaded by the Lord) and the balance of karma and jñāna.
The Jagannath Temple in Puri is associated with Lord Jagannath (a form of Vishnu) as its presiding deity.
The Jagannath Temple in Puri celebrates the Ratha Yatra as its most famous festival.
The Jagannātha Purī Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Jagannātha.
The Jagannātha Temple celebrates the Ratha-yātrā as its most famous festival.
The Jagannath Temple at Puri belongs to the Vaiṣṇava tradition, dedicated to Viṣṇu as Jagannātha.
The Jambukeswarar Temple in Tiruvanaikaval is associated with Lord Shiva as Jambukeswarar.
The Jyotirmaṭha Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Narasiṃha.
The Jvālāmukhī Temple is one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas, where the tongue of Devī fell; famous for the eternal flame emerging from the rock.
The Jvālāmukhī Temple belongs to the Śākta tradition; one of the fifteen Maha Shakti Peethas renowned for its jvālā (flame).
The Kailāsa Giri Temple is associated with Viṣṇu as Nārāyaṇa.
The Kālīghāṭ Temple is one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas, where the right toe of Devī fell; a major center of Kālī worship in Kolkata.
The Kālīghāṭ Temple celebrates Dīpāvalī (Kālī Pūjā) as its primary annual festival during the Amāvasyā.
The Kālīghāṭ Temple belongs to the Śākta tradition; one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas and a major Kālī pilgrimage site in Kolkata.
The Kāmākhyā Temple is one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas, where the yoni of Devī fell; a major center of Tantric Śākta worship in Assam.
The Kāmākhyā Temple celebrates Navarātri with special pūjās over nine nights, culminating in the main annual festival.
The Kāmākhyā Temple belongs to the Śākta tradition as one of the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas and the most important Tantric center in Assam.
The Kāñcī Kāmakōṭi Pīṭham is a Śakti Pīṭha-adjacent center in Kāñcīpuṟam, associated with the Śākta tradition and Kāmākṣī Amman Temple.
The Kāñcī Kāmakōṭi Pīṭham belongs to the Śākta tradition; the adjacent Kāmākṣī Amman Temple is a major Śakti shrine.
The Varadarāja Perumal Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Varadarāja.
The Kashi Vishwanath Temple is associated with Lord Shiva as one of the twelve Jyotirlinga sites.
The Kashi Vishwanath Temple celebrates Mahāśivarātri as a major festival.
The Kashi Vishwanath Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition as one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas.

Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the dialogue between Naciketā and Yama, teaching the distinction between śreyaḥ and preyaḥ, the chariot analogy (body-chariot, senses-horses, mind-reins, intellect-charioteer, ātman-master), and the na jāyate mriyate vā verse.
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad teaches the nature of the ātman (self) through the chariot analogy and the distinction between the eternal and the ephemeral.
The Kedarnath Temple in the Himalayas is associated with Lord Shiva as one of the twelve Jyotirlinga sites and one of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites.
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Kena Upaniṣad, teaching the paradox of the Brahman that cannot be known by the senses/mind but is the knower behind them (pratibodha-viditam).
The Konark Sun Temple is associated with Surya, the Sun God.
The Mahābhārata contains the Anuśāsana Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Āśramavāsika Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Bhīṣma Parva (with Bhagavad Gītā).
The Mahābhārata contains the Droṇa Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Karṇa Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Mahāprasthānika Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Mausala Parva.
The Mahābhārata is divided into 18 major parvas (books) plus a supplement, covering the epic narrative from lineage to war and aftermath.
The Mahābhārata contains the Sabhā Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Sauptika Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Śalya Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Śānti Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Strī Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Svargārohaṇa Parva.
The Mahābhārata contains the Udyoga Parva.
Vana Parva: the Pandavas' 12 years of forest exile, including their exploits such as the story of Arjuna and the Nivātakaṇṭa, and the celestial pilgrimage.
The Mahābhārata contains the Virāṭa Parva.

The Mahākāleśvara Temple at Ujjain is one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas, dedicated to Śiva as Mahākāla in his fierce form; the temple is unique for its south-facing (dakṣiṇāmukhī) liṅga and the Bhasma Ārati ritual.
The Mahākāleśvara Temple celebrates Mahāśivarātri with the Bhasma Ārati, the most prominent Śaiva festival at Ujjain.
The Mahākāleśvara Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition as a Dakṣiṇāmūrti Pīṭha; it is especially sacred during Mahāśivarātri and the Simhastha Kumbha Mela.

Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (with Gauḍapāda's Kārikā), the shortest Upaniṣad (12 verses), analyzing the four states (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya) and the Oṃkāra as the symbol of Brahman.
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad teaches the nature of Brahman as the fourth state (turīya) beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The Meenakshi Amman Temple is associated with Goddess Meenakshi (a form of Devī/Durgā) as its presiding deity.
The Meenakshi Amman Temple celebrates Navaratri as a major festival with the Golu display.
The Meenakshi Amman Temple belongs to the Śākta tradition, being dedicated to the Goddess Meenakshi (Durgā).
Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, distinguishing parā and aparā vidyā, the two birds on a tree (jīvātman and paramātman), and the famous satyam eva jayate mahāvākya.
The Nāgeśvara Temple near Dwarka is one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas, dedicated to Śiva as the lord of serpents; located near the Dwarkadhish Temple.
The Nāgeśvara Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition as one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas; its association with the Puruṣa arca and the nearby Dvārakādhīśa.
The Omkāreśvara Temple on Mandhata Island is one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas, dedicated to Śiva as Omkāra in an Om-shaped island setting on the Narmadā river.
The Omkāreśvara Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition; its location on the Narmadā river and the adjacent Mamleshwar Temple form a sacred pair.

Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Praśna Upaniṣad, structured as six questions (praśnas) from students to Pippalāda, covering prāṇa, the senses, the ātman, sleep/dreams, Oṃ, and the sixteen parts of the puruṣa.
The Āgni Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, an encyclopedic text covering cosmology, iconography, medicine, and Dharmaśāstra.
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a major Vaiṣṇava text in twelve skandhas central to the Gauḍīya tradition.
The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, containing prophecies and historical accounts including those of the Gupta period.
The Brahmā Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Śaiva text with extensive material on pilgrimage sites in North India.
The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Śaiva text describing the structure of the universe (Brahmāṇḍa).
The Garuḍa Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Vaiṣṇava text focusing on Viṣṇu, Garuḍa, and the afterlife (preta-siddhānta).
The Kūrma Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Vaiṣṇava text dedicated to the turtle incarnation of Viṣṇu.
The Liṅga Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Śaiva text devoted to the liṅga form of Śiva.
The Matsya Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Vaiṣṇava text focusing on the fish incarnation of Viṣṇu.
The Nārada Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, focusing on devotion (bhakti) and social topics.
The Padma Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Vaiṣṇava text containing the famous Goṣāṣṇa-darpaṇaṇḍana.
The Śiva Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a major Śaiva text focusing on Shiva's manifestations and the Purāṇic discourse.
The Skanda Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, one of the largest texts covering North and South India, with the Pañcāśa-kuṇḍa stotra.
The Vāmana Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, focusing on the Vāmana (dwarf) incarnation of Viṣṇu.
The Varāha Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, focusing on the Varāha (boar) incarnation of Viṣṇu.
The Vāyu Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, a Śaiva text associated with the wind god, containing the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
The Viṣṇu Purāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, focusing on Viṣṇu's avatars and the genealogy of the solar dynasty.
The Āditya Upapurāṇa focuses on the Āditya (solar) lineage of Viṣṇu.
The Auśanasa Upapurāṇa focuses on teachings of the sage Auśanasa.
The Bhārgava Upapurāṇa focuses on teachings of the sage Bhārgava.
The Garga Upapurāṇa focuses on teachings of the sage Garga.
The Kālikā Upapurāṇa focuses on Kālī worship and Śākta traditions.
The Kapila Upapurāṇa focuses on the sage Kapila, founder of the Sāṅkhya school.
The Mānava Upapurāṇa focuses on teachings of the sage Manu.
The Upapurāṇas include the Matsya Upapurāṇa.
The Nandi Upapurāṇa focuses on the bull Nandi and Śaiva theology.
The Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya Upapurāṇa focuses on the Narasiṃha avatar and Tāpinī practices.
The Nṛsiṃha Upapurāṇa focuses on the Narasiṃha (man-lion) avatar of Viṣṇu.
The Sāmba Upapurāṇa focuses on Sāmba (son of Kṛṣṇa) and Vaiṣṇava theology.
The Saura Upapurāṇa focuses on the Saura (solar) tradition and Sūrya worship.
The Upapurāṇas include the Varāha Upapurāṇa.
The Viṣṇu Dharmottara Upapurāṇa contains Dharmaśāstra, iconography, and artistic guidelines.
Araṇya Kāṇḍa: the Pandavas' forest exile, their encounter with the sage Viśrāma, and the battle with the demon Virupakṣa.
Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa: the exile of Rāma to the forest, the death of Daśaratha, and the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa.
The Rāmāyaṇa contains the Bāla Kāṇḍa.
Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa: Rāma's alliance with Sugrīva, the search for Sītā in the forest, and the division of the earth.
Sundara Kāṇḍa: Hanumān's journey to Lanka, his discovery of Sītā in the Ashoka grove, and his return to Rāma.
Uttara Kāṇḍa: the later life of Rāma, Sītā's exile and return, and the birth of Lava and Kuśa.
Yuddha Kāṇḍa: the great war between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, the death of Rāvaṇa, and Sītā's test of purity (Pariksha).
The Rāmeśvaram Temple also houses the Rāmanāthaliṅga (Śiva), one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas.
The Rāmeśvaram Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Rāmanātha.
The Rāmeśvaram Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition as one of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas (Rāmanāthaliṅga) and one of the four Pañcadvāra Dhāmas.
Maṇḍala 1 of the Ṛgveda contains the famous Nāsadīya Sūkta describing the origin of creation.
Maṇḍala 10 of the Ṛgveda contains the famous Puruṣa Sūkta, the Hymn of the Dead (Narāyaṇa Sūkta), and the creation hymn (Hymn of the Cosmic Being).
Maṇḍala 2 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns addressed to Indra and other deities.
Maṇḍala 3 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Agni, Indra, and other deities, including the Viṣṇu Sūkta.
Maṇḍala 4 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Agni and other deities.
Maṇḍala 5 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Agni, Indra, and the Āditya clan deities.
Maṇḍala 6 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Indra, Agni, and other deities.
Maṇḍala 7 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Indra, Agni, and Varuṇa.
Maṇḍala 8 of the Ṛgveda contains hymns to Agni, Indra, and the Maruts.
Maṇḍala 9 of the Ṛgveda contains the famous Puruṣa Sūkta and hymns to the cosmic order (Ṛta).
The Sabarimala Temple is associated with Lord Ayyappa as its presiding deity.
The Sabarimala Temple pilgrimage season begins with Mahāśivarātri.
The Sabarimala Temple belongs to the Śaiva tradition through its association with Lord Ayyappa (son of Śiva).
The Sāmaveda is associated with several śākhās, including the Jaiminīya and Śāukla recensions.
Lord Shiva is celebrated during Mahāśivarātri, the great night of Shiva.
The Śṛṅgerī Maṭha is associated with the Śakti Pīṭha tradition through its connection to the Devi Bhāgavata tradition.
The Śṛṅgerī Maṭha has Śākta connections through its lineage associations with the Śakti tradition.

Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya on the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, a later Upaniṣad with strong Śaiva orientation, teaching the unity of Rudra and Brahman, the three guṇas, the wheel of saṃsāra, and the path of devotion (bhakti) to Śiva as the supreme.
The Varāha Narasiṃha Temple at Simhācalam is associated with Viṣṇu as Narasiṃha.
The Somnath Temple in Gujarat is associated with Lord Shiva as one of the twelve Jyotirlinga sites.
The Śrīraṅgam Divya Deśam is associated with Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha.
The Śrīraṅgam Temple celebrates Vaikuṇṭha Ekādaśī (Deva Uthani Ekadashi) as its most important 21-day festival.
The Śrīraṅgam Ranganatha Temple belongs to the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, associated with Rāmānuja.

Madhva's Bhāṣya on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, interpreting the five kośas as real gradations of being under Viṣṇu's control, the ānanda-mīmāṃsā as establishing hierarchical bliss, and the bhṛgu-vallī as the jīva's progressive service to Viṣṇu.

Rāmānuja's Bhāṣya on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, interpreting the five kośas as real attributes of Brahman, the ānanda-mīmāṃsā as establishing graded bliss in Brahman's manifestations, and the bhṛgu-vallī as the progressive realization of Viṣṇu as the supreme.
